title: Exception Handling
relevance: Interviewers probe C++ exception mechanics—catch-by-const-reference, stack unwinding/RAII, noexcept, and exception-safety guarantees—as core language fundamentals for robust SDE code.

phases.goal: Establish try/throw/catch, the catch-by-const-reference idiom, the standard exception hierarchy, ordered multi-catch, and catch-all/rethrow.

must_hit.point: Exception handling uses throw to signal an error, try to enclose code that may throw, and catch to handle a matching exception type.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the three keywords and their roles: signal, enclose risky code, handle by type.

must_hit.point: The standard idiom is to throw exception objects and catch them by const reference to avoid copy overhead and object slicing.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says catch (const T& e) / const std::exception&; mentions slicing or lost dynamic type if catching by value.

must_hit.point: std::exception has two main branches: std::logic_error for preventable programmer errors and std::runtime_error for errors hard to predict before run; what() returns a const char* description.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts logic_error (e.g. invalid_argument, out_of_range) with runtime_error (e.g. overflow/underflow) and mentions virtual what().

must_hit.point: Multiple catch blocks are tried in declaration order; most-derived handlers must come before base-class handlers or the base intercepts everything.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States order matters: out_of_range before logic_error before exception; base-first makes later catches unreachable.

must_hit.point: catch (...) catches any exception; a bare throw; rethrows the exact same exception object up the chain.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Distinguishes catch-all for cleanup/logging from bare throw; that preserves original type and state.

probes: Walk through try, throw, and catch: what each does, and why we catch standard exceptions by const reference.
How should you order multiple catch blocks for out_of_range, logic_error, and exception—and what is catch (...) for?

hints.1: Start from the three keywords and what happens when throw runs.
hints.2: Tie the idiom to copying/slicing, then the logic_error vs runtime_error split and catch order.
hints.3: Best practice is catch (const std::exception& e); put most-derived catches first; use catch (...) plus bare throw; to log and propagate.

phases.goal: Explain stack unwinding with RAII, constructor/destructor throw rules, and noexcept behavior.

must_hit.point: Stack unwinding pops frames searching for a matching catch and runs destructors of fully constructed automatic objects in reverse order of creation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes climbing the call stack and automatic destructor calls for abandoned locals before the handler runs.

must_hit.point: RAII ties resource lifetime to objects so unwinding releases memory, files, and locks held in types like unique_ptr or lock_guard.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links unwinding’s destructor calls to leak-free cleanup via RAII wrappers.

must_hit.point: If a constructor throws, that object’s destructor is not called, but destructors of fully constructed members and bases still run.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Object never fully built → no dtor for it; already-built subobjects cleaned up; raw new in ctor can leak, smart pointers do not.

must_hit.point: An exception escaping a destructor during unwinding leaves two active exceptions and the runtime calls std::terminate().
must_hit.evidence_hint: Never let exceptions escape destructors; wrap possibly-throwing dtor work in local try/catch that swallows.

must_hit.point: noexcept promises a function will not throw; violating it calls std::terminate(); destructors are implicitly noexcept; the noexcept operator is a compile-time check.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates the specifier (optimize / terminate on violation) from the operator (true if expression cannot throw); mentions implicit noexcept on destructors.

probes: What is stack unwinding, and how does RAII keep resources safe when an exception propagates?
What happens if a constructor throws versus if a destructor throws during unwinding? When would you mark a function noexcept?

hints.1: Picture the call stack being searched while local objects are destroyed on the way up.
hints.2: Contrast incomplete construction (no object dtor) with a throwing dtor during an already-active exception.
hints.3: Unwinding runs dtors in reverse creation order; ctor-throw skips that object’s dtor; dtor-throw → std::terminate(); noexcept violation also terminates.

phases.goal: Classify exception-safety guarantees and the catch/rethrow choices that preserve type and program state.

must_hit.point: Nothrow/no-fail means the function never throws and is required for destructors and swap; strong means commit-or-rollback with unchanged state on failure.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names nothrow for dtors/swap and strong as all-or-nothing rollback semantics.

must_hit.point: Basic guarantee: on throw, no leaks and invariants hold, but state may be valid yet unpredictable; no guarantee (leaks/corruption) is unacceptable in modern C++.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts basic (valid, possibly messy) with no guarantee (corrupt/leak).

must_hit.point: Prefer bare throw; over throw e; after catching e, because throw e; slices and throws a new copy of the static type.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Bare throw; keeps exact original object; throw e; loses derived type via slicing.

probes: Define the nothrow, strong, and basic exception-safety guarantees—and which apply to destructors and swap.
Inside a catch, when should you write throw; instead of throw e;?

hints.1: Think in levels of what the caller can assume if the function throws.
hints.2: Map nothrow → never throws; strong → unchanged state; basic → valid but maybe changed.
hints.3: Destructors/swap need nothrow; strong is commit-or-rollback; use bare throw; so you do not slice.

phases.goal: Apply hierarchy and RAII in practice: custom exceptions, no finally, and classic interview traps.

must_hit.point: Custom exceptions typically inherit from std::runtime_error (or another suitable standard type) and pass a message to the base constructor.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Sketch inheriting from runtime_error, forwarding msg to the base, optionally adding domain fields.

must_hit.point: C++ has no finally; cleanup relies on RAII so destructors run on both success and exception paths.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts Python try/except/finally with C++ RAII for guaranteed cleanup.

must_hit.point: Constructors should throw to signal failed initialization because they have no return type; prefer RAII members so partial construction does not leak.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Throw from ctor when valid state cannot be built; smart-pointer/RAII members clean up if a later step throws.

probes: How would you write a domain-specific exception type, and how do you guarantee cleanup without finally?
Why is throwing from a constructor the right failure signal, and what resource style should members use?

hints.1: Reuse the standard hierarchy instead of inventing an unrelated root type.
hints.2: Inherit from runtime_error, forward the message, and manage resources with RAII objects.
hints.3: class MyError : public std::runtime_error { ... }; no finally—destructors/RAII clean up; ctor throw = only failure channel, with RAII members.

tradeoffs.topic: Catch by value vs catch by const reference
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Catching by value copies and can slice a derived exception to the base static type; catching by const reference avoids the copy and preserves the polymorphic dynamic type—the standard idiom.
Bare throw; rethrows the exact same exception object with original type and state; throw e; throws a new copy sliced to e’s static type.
Strong is commit-or-rollback: on throw, program state is unchanged as if the call never happened; basic only promises no leaks and preserved invariants, with state possibly changed but still valid.
Python uses finally for cleanup on success or failure; C++ has no finally and relies on RAII so stack unwinding runs destructors and releases resources automatically.

gotchas.trap: Putting a base-class catch before more-derived catches.
gotchas.correction: Handlers are matched in order; a base catch intercepts derived exceptions and later catches become unreachable—most-derived first, bases last.
By-value catch copies and can slice; catch by const reference to avoid copy overhead and keep the dynamic type.

gotchas.trap: Using throw e; to propagate after catch (T& e).
gotchas.correction: That slices and throws a new static-typed copy; use bare throw; to rethrow the original object.

gotchas.trap: Letting an exception escape a destructor, especially during unwinding.
gotchas.correction: A second active exception during unwinding is unresolvable; the runtime calls std::terminate(). Swallow throwing work in a local try/catch inside the destructor.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a constructor-thrown object still runs its destructor.
gotchas.correction: The object was never fully constructed, so its destructor is not called; only fully constructed bases/members are destroyed—use RAII members, not raw owning pointers.

gotchas.trap: Throwing out of a noexcept function.
gotchas.correction: Violating the noexcept promise immediately calls std::terminate(); destructors are implicitly noexcept by default.
